Disappearing Lines

ParadoxesInvariantsGeometry
Game: Two triangles share a row of upright lines; slide the top one and watch one line disappear without any being erased.
How to play: Drag the dot on the top triangle, or focus it and use the arrow keys. You can also press the arrow buttons or "Show the trick" to slide it up and right one notch.
Look for the math

Martin Gardner told this trick in Aha! Gotcha, and Bogomolny made it move. Count the upright lines in the first picture, then slide the top triangle up and to the right by exactly one notch: the same strokes now make one line fewer. Nothing was rubbed out. This is a lesson in conservation: watch what happens to the lengths, not just to the shapes your eyes count.

Build the two triangles

Let the notch size be s. The lower triangle has a vertical stroke at x = r.x + i·s for i = 1, …, N, of length (i−1)·s: it starts s above the bottom edge and ends on the rising diagonal. The upper triangle is the same shape turned upside down and moved to the corner (r.x + s, r.y − s). The applet chooses s = 2 · floor((ceil(W/(2N+1) + 0.5))/2) from a 400-pixel-wide canvas: s = 20 for 10 lines, 36 for 5 and 8 for 25. The numbers of lines the selector offers are exactly 5 through 25, the applet's limits.

One line becomes two halves

At the start, each upper stroke shares its x with a lower stroke and continues it upward, making N long lines of length N·s. After the slide, the upper strokes sit one notch to the right of the lower ones. The first upper and the first lower stroke now have length zero — they have become a single point at opposite corners — and the N−1 remaining strokes pair into N−1 lines of the same length N·s. Two triangles' worth of 2N strokes are still drawn; your eyes just group them differently.

The length never changes

Each half has strokes of lengths 0, s, 2s, …, (N−1)s, so together they always total 2 × (0 + 1 + … + (N−1))s = N(N−1)s pixels. At the start they pair into N lines of length N·s, giving N(N−1)s; after the slide they make N−1 lines of the same length, and the two vanished strokes had length zero, so the total is the same. The page's claim that "the total length of the newly obtained lines is the same as the total length of the original ones" holds: the checks confirm it for every notch size and every snapped position, not only the two pictures on the page. Only the sideways notch changes the count; the upward slide is what makes the applet's three pairs of eyes open, its own reward for finding the exact corner described on the page.

Try 5 lines and then 25: the fewer the lines, the longer the notch and the easier it is to follow a single stroke as it moves. Count the lines before and after the slide, then measure the long ones.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
